content: 1. Laboratory technicians can utilize the shape of urinary crystals to determine their chemical composition. 2. A normal urinalysis does not exclude flank pain caused by cardiac, intra-abdominal, musculoskeletal, or psychological etiologies. 3. Initial diagnostic tests for flank pain should include parameters such as urine pH, white blood cells (WBCs), red blood cells (RBCs), bacteria, casts, and crystals. 4. An alkaline urine pH may indicate infection due to urea-splitting bacteria like Proteus, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, or coagulase-negative Staphylococcus. 5. An acidic urine pH predisposes patients to the formation of uric acid stones. 6. The presence of WBCs in urine suggests infection or inflammation caused by stones, while WBC casts strongly indicate urinary tract infection or acute pyelonephritis. 7. The presence of RBCs in urine is often associated with urinary tract tumors, which can cause gross hematuria, or with stones, which can also lead to hematuria. 8. A repeat urinalysis is necessary after a patient passes a stone to rule out underlying urologic malignancy. 9. If RBCs persist in the urine after stone passage, a urologic evaluation is warranted. 10. A Gram stain can be performed in the emergency room or clinic to detect the presence of infection. 11. A negative Gram stain indicates sterile urine, while the presence of bacteria in an unspun urine specimen suggests infection. 12. Most urinary tract infections are caused by Gram-negative bacteria such as Escherichia coli, though Gram-positive organisms can also be responsible. 13. Urinary calculi are often accompanied by crystals, RBCs, and WBCs in the urine analysis. 14. The shape of urinary crystals can help laboratory technicians identify their composition. 15. A complete blood count (CBC) may reveal leukocytosis, suggesting an infectious etiology, or anemia and abnormal platelet counts, which may indicate bleeding from urologic tumors. 16. Elevated hematocrit levels may be observed in dehydrated states. 17. Serum blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels can be elevated due to renal disease or dehydration. 18. A BUN level greater than 10 times the serum creatinine level suggests dehydration, while a BUN-to-creatinine ratio of 10 or less indicates renal pathology. 19. Serum creatinine levels directly reflect renal function, with elevated levels indicating impaired renal function regardless of BUN values. 20. Abnormal creatinine levels may result from dehydration, obstruction, tumors, infarcts, bilateral renal disease, or solitary kidney disease. 21. Hyponatremia, caused by volume overload, can lead to symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, and seizures. 22. Hyperkalemia may result in cardiac arrhythmias. 23. Serum bicarbonate levels decrease in long-standing renal compromise, often accompanied by hyperkalemia. 24. 25. A beta-hCG test is performed to confirm or rule out pregnancy in females of reproductive age. 26. Positive urine cultures indicate the growth of ≥100,000 colony-forming units/mL of urine, while positive blood cultures are found in 15–30% of cases. 27. A peripheral blood film may show leukocytosis with or without a left shift. 28. A coagulation profile is necessary in cases where surgical intervention is planned. 29. Additional tests, such as antinuclear antibody, perinuclear anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, cytoplasmic anti-neutrophilic antibody, protein C and S levels, Factor V Leiden mutation, anticardiolipin antibody (IgM and IgG), antithrombin III activity, vitamin B12, folic acid, and homocysteine levels, are performed to rule out differential conditions, hypercoagulable states, and thromboembolic events. 30. A plain abdominal X-ray (KUB) can help identify urinary calculi by visualizing the kidneys, ureters, and bladder. 31. The entire X-ray film should be examined for intestinal gas patterns, gallstones, bony structures, and free air, which may provide insights into the etiology of pain. 32. Renal cell carcinomas, which are osteolytic tumors, can be detected radiographically in metastatic stages. 33. Abnormal intestinal gas patterns, gallstones, or free air suggest intra-abdominal pathology. 34. Aortic calcifications and aneurysms should be evaluated to determine if renal artery disease is the cause of flank pain. 35. Urinary calculi appear as calcifications overlying the kidney shadow or along the ureter's course. 36. Small stones (1–2 mm) can cause severe flank pain if they obstruct urinary flow into the bladder. 37. Stones typically become obstructive at the ureteropelvic junction, where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim, or where the ureter enters the bladder. 38. Small stones tend to lodge at the ureterovesical junction (UVJ), while larger stones lodge higher in the urinary tract. 39. Uric acid calculi are radiolucent and not visible on plain abdominal X-rays but can be detected using ultrasound or CT scans. 40. An intravenous pyelogram (IVP) is a cost-effective functional study that diagnoses most urologic, infectious, and cardiac causes of flank pain. 41. IVP is indicated when renal ultrasound and non-contrast CT scans do not assess renal function. 42. In cases where renal ultrasound and non-contrast CT scans show no abnormalities, but renal infarction due to arterial embolism is suspected, IVP can assess renal function.
